opus_only: The lookback-straddle model is offered as a basis for trend-following fund benchmarks.
Hedge funds do not disclose their activities and LTCM (1998) raised concern about their hidden risk, motivating a model of strategy risk.
Because funds dynamically mix several nonlinear strategies, studying a general hedge fund sample is of limited value; one should model a single strategy that many funds follow.
Footnote 3: option-like return features are found even among mutual funds (Lehman and Modest 1987).
Trading rules are proprietary, so the authors can only theorise what trend followers do rather than estimate risk directly.
Footnote 5: CTAs are CFTC-registered advisors (via NFA membership) who trade mainly futures for clients.
The convex pattern in Figure 1 resembles a straddle payout on the underlying asset.
Three-month options are used because they are the most liquid, although this horizon may be too short to separate lookback from standard straddles.
The goal is only to show that one bills-plus-lookback-straddle portfolio behaves like trend followers; other option portfolios might replicate better.
Data: futures and options from the Futures Industry Institute (DTB, MATIF, Osaka, CME options), the exchanges (LIFFE, SFE, TIFFE; CBOT/NYMEX options) and Datastream (CBOT, CME, NYMEX futures).
Figure 3 (read from chart): with a steady rise into expiry both straddles end at similar levels (about 220-230 from 100).
Trend-following fund returns correlate strongly with PTFS returns, which means they carry systematic risk that linear models on asset indices miss.
The five PTFS portfolios explain 47.9% of trend-following returns, mostly via currencies and commodities; the joint F-test of no relation is rejected decisively.
In those crash periods stock PTFSs paid off as expected, and so did most bond, currency and commodity PTFSs, but fewer than half of the short-rate PTFSs.
Commodity PTFSs do not show the option-like pattern versus world equities.
Financial assets (stocks, bonds, short rates, currencies) react to the same macro events, so extreme equity moves coincide with large moves, and trend profits, in the other financial markets.

Table 4: in the worst equity state stock PTFS +12.8%, bond +5.9%, currency +8.3%, short-rate +8.3%, commodity +1.2%, funds +2.0%; in the best state +9.4%, +10.2%, +8.2%, +5.6%, -2.5%, funds +5.7%; in the middle state most PTFSs lose about 1-5.5%.
To compare with survey data the authors assume the 41.2% bonds/short-rate share splits evenly.

Feature 2: extreme-period fund returns are explained by PTFSs on DEM and JPY, wheat and silver, Eurodollar and Short Sterling, and US bonds, but not stock indices; PTFSs beat buy-and-hold and industry benchmarks.
sonnet_only: Disclosure: research was supported by a managed-futures foundation and by John W. Henry & Company, a large trend-following CTA, a potential conflict to bear in mind.
Linear models can make hedge funds look as if they have no systematic risk, because the risk is nonlinear.
Hedge funds dynamically allocate across strategies with different nonlinear risks, so pooled samples blur risk; the authors instead study one identifiable strategy (trend following, CTA funds).
Trend following is the self-described strategy of most CTAs (Billingsley and Chance 1996), so CTA funds are used as the sample.
Caveat: trading rules are proprietary, so the model is a theoretical proxy, not a replication of any manager.
The key empirical link: lookback straddle returns resemble trend-following fund returns, connecting funds to standard asset markets.
Theory (Section 1, Appendix A): a lookback straddle captures trend following better than a standard straddle, which captures market timing.
Both primitive strategies complete a single trade per interval, following Merton (1981).
Universe, commodities: soybean, wheat, corn (CBOT), gold, silver, crude oil (NYMEX).
Data: exchange-supplied or purchased futures and options settlement data plus Datastream futures (Appendix B).
Lookback straddle is used in all empirical tests, chosen on theory rather than empirical superiority.
The authors flag a positive implicit alpha in trend-following funds relative to PTFS, deferring analysis (Section 4 does not actually quantify it).
Funds' mean exceeds nearly every individual PTFS mean with greater statistical significance.
Regression of trend-following funds on the five PTFS portfolios gives adjusted R2 of 47.9%, with currency and commodity PTFS largest; the F-test rejects no relation.
Interpretation: trend followers have systematic risk that linear models on standard benchmarks miss but PTFS capture.
In the two equity crashes the bond, currency and commodity PTFS mostly earned positive returns, not just stocks.
Table 4 note: state sizes differ from the text (note says state 5 has the best 34 months and state 3 the remaining 30; text says best 30 and remaining 34), an inconsistency in the table notes.
Table 4 numbers: by state 1-5 trend-following funds earn +2.03%, +1.12%, +1.32%, +0.10%, +5.69% a month versus MS World -4.60%, -0.59%, +1.56%, +3.36%, +6.74%.
Interpretation: currency is the most popular trend-following market and stocks the least.
Individual-fund test sample: 163 trend-following funds with at least 24 months of returns to end-1997, regressed on five buy-and-hold portfolios and on the five PTFS portfolios.
Out-of-sample support: in Q3 1998 the S&P declined more than 10% while the vast majority of trend-following funds made large gains.
Q3 1998 out-of-sample: most trend-following funds made large gains during the S&P decline.
Standard straddle delta equals a market timer who compares the current price only to the starting price.
Reference list: Fung and Hsieh (1997a,b), Glosten and Jagannathan (1994), Goldman-Sosin-Gatto (1979), Merton (1981), Billingsley and Chance (1996); no new evidence.
